Speech by Vice Chair for Supervision Bowman on modernizing banking supervision: a shared agenda for the Americas - Federal Reserve (.gov)
Bowman, Modernizing Banking Supervision: A Shared Agenda for the Americas
headlines.officialText: To be effective in this work, bank supervisory and regulatory frameworks must be forward looking to anticipate future risks. Recent experience in the United States demonstrates that it is not sufficient to identify financial risks. Supervisors must also have the authority, accountability, and judgment to act before those risks are realized. These frameworks must focus on the most material risks, enable timely decisions, and adapt to rapidly changing financial markets and technologies. The review validated that supervisors identified the bank's fundamental vulnerabilities well before its failure.2 Those vulnerabilities included substantial interest rate risk, a highly concentrated and predominantly uninsured deposit base, and inadequate preparedness to meet liquidity demands. These were not unfamiliar or complicated risks to understand. They have been common risks throughout history, were present at the time of SVB's failure, and continue to be fundamental banking risks today. But the process did not result in prompt action to require the bank to address material risks that ultimately led to its failure. Yet no finding required SVB to shorten the maturity profile of its securities portfolio or restructure the held-to-maturity book, which were material financial risks that contributed to the bank's failure. While interest rate risk was discussed, the approach criticized how the bank measured the risk but did not direct the bank to reduce it. But the risks that were most material—the risks that affected the bank's financial condition—were not addressed. Instead, we must measure success by whether our work results in the timely identification, mitigation, and remediation of material risks. Artificial intelligence (or super intelligence), advanced analytics, and other supervisory technologies have the potential to improve the identification of emerging risks and our understanding of complex financial relationships. The ultimate measure of successful and effective supervision is the ability to recognize material risks and act effectively while there is still time to influence the outcome. Modernizing Our Supervisory and Regulatory Frameworks Second, we must ensure our regulatory and supervisory frameworks enable the identification of material risks, sound decisionmaking, and supervisory response in a rapidly changing financial system. Our priorities should be to ensure supervisors are trained to identify and focus attention on material risks, enable timely decisionmaking and clear accountability, and establish a regulatory framework that encourages innovation without compromising safety and soundness. Our Statement of Supervisory Operating Principles refocuses supervision on identifying material risks and taking prompt, proportionate action to address them. They also seek to align examination findings and supervisory ratings more closely with material risks, reduce unnecessary duplication, and streamline the resolution of supervisory concerns. It is to ensure that supervision identifies the risks that matter most and results in timely action to address them.3 Second, we are changing how we organize the supervisory function itself. Our responsibility is to establish clear and predictable rules of the road so that financial institutions can confidently pursue responsible innovation while managing the material risks associated with new activities.
